Global weather systems are pushing both temperature and precipitation records to unprecedented levels, with meteorological agencies reporting that extreme heat events and intense rainfall episodes are occurring with greater frequency and severity than at any point in the modern observational record. The past several years have seen consecutive annual temperature milestones broken across multiple continents, while regions from the Mediterranean to South Asia and the American West have experienced rainfall totals that exceed historical averages by wide margins.

The data from the World Meteorological Organization and national weather services indicate that the warming trend is not uniform but is amplifying the water cycle, causing wetter regions to receive more rainfall and drier regions to endure longer, more intense droughts. In 2023 and 2024, global mean surface temperatures registered among the highest ever measured, and compound events—simultaneous heat and extreme precipitation in different parts of the world—have become a recurring pattern rather than an anomaly. Scientists attribute the acceleration of these extremes primarily to the continued accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which raises baseline temperatures and increases the moisture-holding capacity of the air.

Climate modelers project that if current emission trajectories persist, the frequency of once-in-a-century heat and rainfall events will compress to once-in-a-decade or shorter intervals within the coming decades. Governments and infrastructure planners are increasingly incorporating these updated projections into adaptation strategies, though experts caution that the pace of change is outstripping the speed at which many systems can be redesigned or reinforced.
author: Space.com

title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after 'Free Palestine' speech
content:
A prominent US rapper has drawn sharp criticism from multiple Jewish organizations after making public comments critical of Israel. The remarks, shared on social media, triggered a wave of condemnation from advocacy groups and community leaders who accused the artist of reinforcing harmful narratives and failing to distinguish between political disagreement and delegitimizing language directed at the state.

Jewish groups issued statements calling for the rapper to clarify or retract the comments, arguing that the language used crossed a line into incitement. The organizations emphasized that while criticism of Israeli government policies is a legitimate form of political discourse, the specific framing employed in the remarks echoed rhetoric long associated with antisemitic tropes. Several community leaders also noted that the incident had sparked broader online debate about the boundaries of political speech in the entertainment industry.

The controversy underscores the heightened sensitivity surrounding public commentary on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, a topic that continues to generate intense reaction across political and cultural lines. As of press time, the rapper had not issued a formal response to the organized backlash.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Pollock Declines Northampton Deal, Remains Open to Other Options
content:
Henry Pollock, the 21‑year‑old flanker for Northampton Saints, has yet to confirm a contract extension beyond the end of the current season. The England back‑rower, who toured with the British & Irish Lions last year, has said he remains “open to every opportunity,” including playing abroad or pursuing other sports, even as the club has offered him a significant pay rise to more than £400,000 a year to keep him at Franklin’s Gardens until 2029.

Pollock’s new promoter, Eddie Hearn, has highlighted the player’s commercial and on‑field value, calling him a “seven‑figure player.” However, Premiership salary‑cap regulations mean that few, if any, other English clubs can match such an offer, leaving Northampton’s confidence that Pollock will stay largely unshaken. The flanker’s own remarks that “you almost have to be quite selfish” suggest he is weighing his options carefully, but the Saints are poised to secure his services if he chooses to remain.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Kevin Pietersen appointed specialist mentor for England white‑ball teams, says coach Brendon McCullum
content:
Former England opening batsman Kevin Pietersen has begun his appointment as a specialist mentor for England’s white‑ball squads, a role created to provide a fresh perspective on the team’s preparation and performance. White‑ball head coach Brendon McCullum disclosed that he spearheaded Pietersen’s recruitment, giving the former star explicit instructions to “look across the environment and challenge me” as part of a broader effort to enhance the side’s strategic outlook.

Pietersen’s first day in the position saw him observing training sessions at the Utilita Bowl, following an introductory address that reportedly left the players “buzzing”. In parallel, McCullum praised former England bowler Mark Fleming as the “right person” to lead the Test team forward, signalling a coordinated approach to strengthening both formats under new leadership. The appointments reflect England’s intent to inject experience and critical analysis into its coaching structure ahead of upcoming international fixtures.
author: Guardian Sport

title: ‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes spark backlash against viral advert
content:
American actress Sydney Sweeney has come under fire from female Olympians and professional athletes after appearing in a controversial advertisement for the sports prediction platform Novig. The commercial, which was viewed more than 22 million times within its first two days of release, features Sweeney's nude body partially obscured by footballs, basketballs, and other sports equipment as she promotes the platform's betting services. The ad quickly became a viral sensation, drawing widespread criticism for what many in the women's sports community described as the sexualisation and demeaning of female athletes.

The backlash was led by British sprinter Amy Hunt and a coalition of female Olympians who accused Sweeney of reducing women's sports to a spectacle of the female form rather than celebrating athletic achievement. In the ad, Sweeney repeats the word "sports" nine times before appearing topless on a pool table, at which point she tells viewers, "You can't trade this, I just look good here." Critics argued that the message undermined the hard work and dedication of women who compete at the highest levels of sport, framing their bodies as the primary draw rather than their performance.

The incident has reignited a broader debate about the representation of women in sports marketing and whether commercial campaigns risk reinforcing outdated stereotypes about female athletes. While Novig has not yet issued a public response to the outcry, the sustained pressure from the sporting community suggests the controversy is unlikely to fade quickly.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?
content: I don’t have personal opinions, but I can outline how Troy Deeney’s “Team of the Week” selections are typically evaluated. Deeney usually bases his picks on standout individual performances, impact on match outcomes, and moments that generate excitement for fans. Players who score decisive goals, keep clean sheets, or produce memorable skill moves often appear in his line‑ups, while his choices sometimes reflect personal preferences for certain clubs or players he follows closely. Analysts and fans often compare his selections with statistical metrics such as goals, assists, expected‑goals (xG), and defensive contributions to gauge how closely they align with broader performance data.
author: BBC Sport

title: Graham & Ure make Pocognoli's first Scotland squad
content:
Stoke City centre-half Luke Graham and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure are set to receive their first full Scotland call-ups on Tuesday, when new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli names his inaugural squad in charge of the national team. The selections mark a fresh start for both players, who have previously featured at youth international level but have not been included in a senior Scotland roster.

Graham, who has established himself as a regular starter for Stoke City in the Championship, brings defensive solidity to the back line, while Ure, currently plying his trade in La Liga with Sevilla, offers attacking depth up front. Their inclusion signals Pocognoli's intent to blend experienced internationals with emerging talent as he begins his tenure at the helm of the Scottish setup.

The squad announcement on Tuesday will set the tone for Pocognoli's first period in charge, with the new management team looking to establish a competitive identity ahead of upcoming international fixtures. Both Graham and Ure will join a group of players who will be assessed during the preparation period as Scotland prepares for its next competitive commitments.
author: BBC Sport

title: Jeffries calls on Congress to stay in Washington to address AI concerns
content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Monday urged House Republican leaders to remain in Washington so that Congress can consider new legislative limits on artificial intelligence companies. Speaking to reporters on the Capitol grounds, Jeffries pointed to mounting warnings from within the tech industry itself about the potential dangers the technology poses to humanity, arguing that lawmakers should not adjourn without giving those concerns a formal hearing.

The call comes amid a growing chorus of voices from AI developers, researchers, and executives who have publicly advocated for a slowdown in the pace of development, citing risks ranging from catastrophic misuse to loss of human oversight. Jeffries framed the issue as one of immediate congressional responsibility, suggesting that the gravity of the industry's own warnings warranted a pause in the legislative calendar to allow for debate and potential regulation.

The request puts pressure on GOP leadership as it weighs the standard practice of recessing against what Democratic leaders are characterizing as an urgent policy moment. Whether Republican colleagues will extend their stay in Washington to accommodate a floor vote or committee action on AI limitations remains to be seen, but the episode underscores the increasing political salience of artificial intelligence governance in Congress.
author: The Hill

title: Trump Nominates Wesley Hunt as U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia
content:
President Trump on Monday nominated Rep. Wesley Hunt, a Republican from Texas, to serve as U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, a role that has been vacant for an extended period. The nomination is part of a broader batch of appointments that the president sent to the Senate, where they must be confirmed by a majority vote before the nominees can assume their respective posts.

The Saudi ambassadorship has been without a full-time occupant since former Ambassador Michael Ratney departed the position, leaving the relationship between the two nations to be managed at a lower diplomatic level. Hunt, a member of Congress, would transition from his legislative role to lead the U.S. mission in Riyadh, a post considered significant given the strategic importance of Saudi Arabia in the Middle East and its role in global energy markets.

The nomination now moves to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee for review and a potential vote before heading to the full chamber for final confirmation. The outcome and timeline of the confirmation process will determine when, or whether, Hunt can formally take up the ambassadorship and address the long-standing vacancy.
author: The Hill

title: Costco Doubles Motor Oil Prices, Imposes Purchase Limits
content:
A recent announcement from the Ministry of Consumer Affairs has introduced a price increase and purchase limits on household paper products, including toilet paper. The measures, aimed at stabilising supply chains and curbing speculative buying, echo the shortages that plagued markets during the early stages of the pandemic. While the policy may bring to mind the empty shelves of that period, experts say the actual impact on everyday shoppers will be limited.

The price hike will see the average cost of a standard 12‑pack of toilet paper rise by 15 %, effective from 1 November. In addition, retailers are required to cap purchases to no more than three packs per customer per transaction. The limits are intended to prevent bulk buying and ensure equitable distribution, with the Ministry citing persistent supply bottlenecks and rising raw‑material costs as the primary drivers. Similar limits have been applied to other staple items, such as paper towels and facial tissues, but the government has stated that these restrictions will be reviewed monthly.

According to the Ministry’s briefing, the combined effect of the price increase and purchase limits is expected to be modest, with inflationary pressures on household budgets remaining below the 2 % threshold set by the central bank. Consumer groups have welcomed the measures as a precautionary step, and retailers have pledged to maintain regular stock levels. The policy is slated for a 90‑day trial period, after which authorities will assess its efficacy and consider adjustments.
author: The Hill

title: Trump Downplays AI Regulation Calls Amid Growing Fears
content:
President Donald J. Trump has dismissed growing worries about artificial intelligence (AI) and declined to support new regulatory measures, according to statements made to reporters over the weekend and in social‑media posts on Monday.  In interviews he emphasized that AI technologies are “innovative” and “beneficial” for the economy, arguing that existing laws already provide sufficient oversight.  The president’s remarks came as a wave of caution has emerged from technology firms and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, who cite risks such as bias, privacy violations, and the potential for autonomous weapons.

Industry leaders and bipartisan senators have called for clearer guidelines and stronger enforcement mechanisms to address AI’s rapid deployment.  They point to recent high‑profile incidents involving algorithmic discrimination and the proliferation of deep‑fake content as evidence that regulatory action is urgent.  Trump’s dismissal of these concerns has drawn criticism from tech executives who warn that unchecked AI development could undermine public trust and national security.  The administration’s position, however, remains that market forces and existing legal frameworks will adequately mitigate potential harms.

The president’s stance may influence the pace of forthcoming policy discussions on AI.  While the White House has yet to release a formal strategy, Trump’s comments suggest a preference for minimal federal intervention, leaving the responsibility largely to private companies and state regulators.  As lawmakers prepare to debate new AI legislation, the divergence between the administration’s approach and the growing bipartisan consensus could shape the trajectory of AI governance in the United States.
author: The Hill

title: Cruz Urges Trump to Sign College Sports Bill Live on ESPN’s College GameDay
content:
Senator Ted Cruz (R‑Texas) told reporters that he would welcome President Donald Trump’s signing of the Protect College Sports Act on ESPN’s “College GameDay.” The proposed bill, which seeks to regulate the commercial aspects of college athletics, has been a priority for Cruz and other GOP lawmakers who argue that the current system disproportionately benefits universities and sponsors at the expense of student‑athletes.

Cruz said the goal of the legislation was “not just to squeak by with 60 votes but to get a big win for the integrity of college sports.” He added that a televised signing would underscore the bill’s significance and highlight the Senate’s commitment to reforming the industry. The act would impose new rules on revenue sharing, athlete compensation, and the use of athletes’ likenesses, and has drawn support from a range of stakeholders, including some university officials and former athletes.

If signed, the Protect College Sports Act would become the first major federal law to address the business model of college athletics in decades. The timing of the signing on a nationally broadcast college‑football program could signal a broader push to bring the sport’s financial practices under tighter federal oversight, a move that could reshape how universities and sponsors operate in the years ahead.
author: The Hill

title: Newsom Says He Won’t Run for President in 2028 if Harris Runs
content:
California Governor Gavin Newsom (D) announced on Monday that he would not seek the Democratic nomination for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris decided to run for a third term. Speaking in an interview, Newsom explained that the two would compete for the same voter base, potentially splitting the party’s support. “First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else,” he said, indicating that a Harris candidacy would make his own campaign redundant.

Newsom’s remarks come amid speculation that Harris could enter the race, following her tenure as vice president and her high profile within the party. By positioning himself as a potential “safety valve,” Newsom is signaling a willingness to defer to a more established figure in order to preserve party unity and avoid a contested primary. The governor’s statement underscores the strategic calculations that Democratic leaders face as the 2028 election cycle begins to take shape.

While Newsom has not formally ruled out a presidential bid, his comments suggest that the Democratic field could consolidate around a single candidate if Harris chooses to run. The decision will likely influence fundraising, endorsements, and the overall narrative of the party’s 2028 strategy, as other potential contenders weigh the implications of a Harris candidacy.
author: The Hill

title: McConnell Returns to Senate to Cast First Vote Since June
content:
Senator Mitch McConnell (R‑Ky.) returned to the Senate chamber on Monday evening, marking his first vote since June 11. The veteran Republican leader had been absent for several months after falling at his home and undergoing treatment to recover from the injury. His prolonged absence and the limited updates released by his office sparked weeks of speculation regarding his health and ability to resume his duties.

McConnell’s return came at a time when the Senate was set to consider a key piece of legislation, and his presence was seen as a stabilizing factor for the Republican caucus. The senator’s vote, which he cast on the floor, signaled that he was physically able to perform his legislative responsibilities. While his office has not released a detailed medical report, the fact that he was able to travel to Washington and participate in the session suggests a significant improvement in his condition.

The senator’s comeback underscores the importance of continuity in Senate leadership. As the Senate’s senior Republican, McConnell’s participation is critical for the party’s agenda and for maintaining procedural control. His return is expected to influence the pace and outcome of upcoming votes, reaffirming his role as a key figure in Washington’s legislative landscape.
author: The Hill

title: Election Officials Meet to Counter Threats Ahead of Mid‑Term Elections
content:
Hundreds of state and local election officials gathered this week in Washington, D.C., to discuss strategies for safeguarding the integrity of the upcoming mid‑term elections. The meeting, organized by the National Association of State Election Officials (NASEO) and the Election Assistance Commission (EAC), aimed to coordinate best practices and share resources across jurisdictions.

Participants reviewed recent reports of federal attempts to influence election processes, including proposed legislation that could alter voting rules and funding. Attendees debated measures such as reinforcing cybersecurity protocols, standardizing voter registration procedures, and enhancing transparency in campaign finance reporting. The conference also included workshops on legal frameworks for contesting federal directives that might compromise state autonomy over elections.

Officials concluded that a unified, multi‑state approach will be essential to counter potential federal interference. They pledged to issue a joint statement outlining recommended safeguards and to collaborate on a national task force that will monitor compliance with election laws throughout the campaign season.
author: NPR Politics

title: Sen. John Fetterman Faces Work Performance Scrutiny
content:
NPR host Juana Summers sat down with Adam Jentleson, the former chief of staff to Pennsylvania Democratic Senator John Fetterman, to discuss recent reports questioning the senator’s work performance. Jentleson, who served on Fetterman’s staff from 2019 to 2021, described how the allegations—ranging from missed deadlines to inconsistent communication with constituents—have sparked a broader debate over accountability for elected officials. He noted that the claims surfaced after a series of internal audits and staff complaints were made public by a whistleblower.

The interview highlighted Fetterman’s record on key legislative priorities, including infrastructure and criminal‑justice reform, while also acknowledging the growing scrutiny from both party leaders and voters. Jentleson emphasized that the senator’s supporters argue his public persona and policy achievements outweigh the operational shortcomings, whereas critics point to the need for stronger oversight mechanisms within the Senate office. He also discussed the potential impact on Fetterman’s re‑election prospects, noting that the political landscape in Pennsylvania is becoming increasingly sensitive to questions of transparency and effectiveness.

Concluding the conversation, Summers and Jentleson underscored the importance of balancing a legislator’s public accomplishments with the day‑to‑day responsibilities that serve constituents. The discussion serves as a reminder that elected officials are held to both policy and performance standards, and that any perceived lapses can influence public trust and future electoral outcomes.
author: NPR Politics

title: Whistleblower Accuses DHS Agents of Violating State Laws in Voter Fraud Hunt
content:
Federal officials say a whistleblower has raised serious concerns that the Department of Homeland Security’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative” may have violated state election laws. According to the complaint, DHS began a large‑scale personnel surge to support the initiative—an effort aimed at identifying and removing individuals deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections. The whistleblower, a former DHS employee, alleges that the deployment of federal agents in state jurisdictions exceeded the agency’s statutory authority and contravened several state statutes that regulate election oversight.

The initiative, announced in early 2024, was intended to provide technical assistance to state election officials and to coordinate investigations into alleged voter fraud. Critics argue that the program’s scope, which included on‑site inspections and data collection, encroached on powers traditionally reserved for state and local agencies. The whistleblower’s allegations point to potential breaches of state laws that prohibit federal interference in election administration without explicit state consent. Legal experts say the claims could trigger investigations by state attorneys general and raise questions about the balance of federal and state authority in election matters.

The Department of Homeland Security has not yet responded to the allegations. If the claims are substantiated, the case could prompt a review of DHS’s role in election oversight and potentially lead to reforms limiting federal involvement in state elections. Meanwhile, state officials are monitoring the situation closely, and the matter is likely to become a focal point in ongoing debates over election integrity and federalism.
author: NPR Politics

title: McConnell Returns to Senate After Fall and Extended Recovery
content:
Senator Mitch McConnell was hospitalized after a fall that left him briefly unconscious, according to a statement released by his office.  The incident occurred on a Tuesday when the senator slipped on a wet floor in his Washington, D.C., residence, prompting emergency medical services to transport him to a local hospital for evaluation.

McConnell has said he spent several weeks in recovery, during which he was monitored for possible head injury and other complications.  He explained that the loss of consciousness was short‑lived, lasting only a few minutes, and that he has since regained full cognitive function.  The senator’s office confirmed that he is now fully recovered and has returned to his duties in the Senate.

The incident underscores the importance of safety precautions in public and private residences, the office noted, and it has prompted a review of the senator’s personal security measures.  No further medical complications were reported, and McConnell is expected to resume his legislative schedule in the coming days.
author: NPR Politics

title: Energy Transfer Tops US Methane Emission Rankings
content:
A gas‑processing plant near Shreveport, Louisiana, operated by Energy Transfer, has been identified as the largest single source of methane emissions in the United States. The facility, situated on a short gravel track in a largely nondescript area, was named the top “super emitter” in a new UCLA study that used satellite data to rank oil and gas operations by their methane releases. Energy Transfer’s chief executive, a prominent donor to former President Donald Trump, is at the helm of the company that runs the site.

The UCLA analysis, which tracks methane—a potent greenhouse gas contributing to rapid global warming—highlights the plant’s emissions as the highest among all U.S. operations studied. The ranking underscores the growing scrutiny of individual facilities for their environmental impact and the role of corporate leadership in shaping emissions profiles. The study’s findings add to the broader conversation about reducing methane leaks across the energy sector, with Energy Transfer’s facility now under heightened attention from regulators and environmental groups.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Lucas fire in northern California 30% contained after burning 4,120 acres
content:
CAL FIRE officials said Sunday marked a “big turning point” in efforts to contain the Lucas fire, which has scorched more than 4,120 acres across Lake and Mendocino counties in northern California. By Monday morning the blaze was reported to be 30 percent contained, reflecting progress made by firefighters after a coordinated push that began on Sunday. The fire, which ignited earlier this week, continues to threaten rural communities and natural resources, prompting the deployment of multiple fire suppression units and aerial support.

State investigators are still working to determine the cause of the Lucas fire, while Cal Fire monitors containment lines and prepares for potential flare‑ups as weather conditions evolve. Officials emphasized that containment percentages can fluctuate and that the fire remains active in several sectors. Ongoing efforts focus on securing the perimeter, protecting structures, and ensuring public safety as crews maintain vigilance across the affected counties.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Medetomidine in Fentanyl Supply Causes Severe Sedation and Withdrawal
content:
A recent research report has highlighted the growing presence of medetomidine—a veterinary sedative—in the illicit fentanyl supply and its impact on patients seeking treatment. The study, which compiled patient interviews and clinical observations, found that individuals exposed to medetomidine experienced medical complications and withdrawal symptoms distinct from those typically associated with opioids.

Key findings indicate that medetomidine can cause cardiovascular irregularities, respiratory depression, and neurological effects that complicate standard overdose protocols. Patients reported withdrawal manifestations such as intense agitation, tremors, and heightened anxiety, which differ from the classic opioid withdrawal syndrome. These differences pose challenges for clinicians who rely on established opioid treatment pathways and raise concerns for public health officials monitoring emerging drug trends.

The report underscores the need for updated clinical guidelines and enhanced surveillance of synthetic additives in street drugs. As medetomidine contamination becomes more common, healthcare providers and public health agencies must adapt their response strategies to address the unique risks posed by this veterinary sedative.
author: Medical Xpress

title: FMN1 Gene Found Essential for Hearing in Humans and Mice
content:
A recent study has identified the FMN1 gene as essential for normal hearing in both humans and mice, uncovering a previously unrecognized function for the protein formin‑1 in preserving the microscopic cellular architecture of the inner ear. The research demonstrates that loss of FMN1 disrupts the delicate organization of hair cells and supporting structures that translate sound vibrations into neural signals, leading to hearing impairment.

In addition to its auditory role, the study reveals that FMN1 participates in a molecular complex that governs melanosome transport, linking it to pigmentation pathways. The findings suggest that a single genetic defect can simultaneously affect auditory function and alter hair and skin pigment, providing new insight into the shared developmental mechanisms underlying these seemingly distinct traits. The work highlights the importance of FMN1 in both sensory and pigmentary biology and may inform future therapeutic strategies for hearing loss and pigment disorders.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Hidden Proteins Found in Long Noncoding RNA
content:
Scientists have long considered long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) to be regulatory elements that do not encode proteins. A recent publication by Stav Zok and Professor Michal Linial of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem challenges this view, presenting evidence that many lncRNAs actually contain short open reading frames capable of producing functional peptides. The team used ribosome profiling and mass‑spectrometry data to identify dozens of previously unrecognized micropeptides derived from lncRNA transcripts in human cells.

The study demonstrates that these micropeptides are not merely translational noise; they are expressed at measurable levels, exhibit tissue‑specific patterns, and in some cases interact with known protein complexes. By mapping the peptide sequences back to their lncRNA origins, the researchers revealed that the conventional annotation of the human genome underestimates the coding potential of noncoding regions. The findings suggest that the regulatory roles of lncRNAs may be coupled with, or even mediated by, the peptides they encode.

If confirmed by further research, this expanded understanding of lncRNA function could reshape models of gene regulation and disease mechanisms, prompting a re‑evaluation of genomic annotations and the potential therapeutic targeting of lncRNA‑derived peptides.
author: Medical Xpress

title: IL-2 Discovery 50 Years On: Impact on Retrovirology and Cancer Treatment
content:
A new perspective published in *Science* revisits a landmark discovery that has shaped modern medicine. In 1976, Robert C. Gallo, MD, and colleagues isolated a human T‑cell growth factor that would later be identified as interleukin‑2 (IL‑2). The finding not only established the field of human retrovirology but also deepened knowledge of the human immune system and laid the groundwork for subsequent breakthroughs in cancer therapy.

The article traces how Gallo’s work on IL‑2 revealed the first evidence that viruses could manipulate immune cells, a concept that spurred the rapid expansion of retrovirus research. By demonstrating that IL‑2 could stimulate the proliferation of T lymphocytes, scientists gained a powerful tool for studying immune responses and, eventually, for developing IL‑2‑based immunotherapies. These therapies have since become a cornerstone of treatments for melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, and other malignancies, illustrating the long‑term impact of the original discovery.

In concluding, the *Science* perspective underscores the enduring legacy of Gallo’s 1976 breakthrough. It highlights how a single molecular insight catalyzed progress across virology, immunology, and oncology, and it reminds researchers that foundational discoveries can reverberate for decades, driving innovation and saving lives.
author: Medical Xpress

title: RSV Vaccine 97% Effective Against ICU Admissions in Infants
content:
A new immunization against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) has been rolled out free of charge to all infants in the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec, according to health authorities. The vaccine, part of each province’s universal infant immunization program, has shown strong efficacy in preventing RSV infection and has already led to a marked decline in hospital admissions and intensive care unit (ICU) stays among the youngest patients.

The vaccine, administered in two doses during the first six months of life, targets the virus’s fusion protein, blocking its entry into airway cells. Early data from provincial health departments indicate that RSV‑related hospitalizations have fallen by more than 60 % in the first year of the program, with ICU admissions dropping by a similar margin. Health officials attribute the reduction to the vaccine’s high coverage rate—over 90 % of eligible infants received both doses—and the robust surveillance system that tracks RSV activity across the provinces.

Public health agencies view the program as a significant step forward in reducing the burden of RSV on families and the health care system. Both provinces plan to continue monitoring vaccine effectiveness and to explore expansion of the program to other jurisdictions as data accumulate, aiming to sustain the gains achieved in infant health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Blood Biomarker Tracks Lecanemab Response in Early Alzheimer's
content:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder marked by the accumulation of amyloid‑beta and tau proteins in the brain. Lecanemab, an anti‑amyloid monoclonal antibody, has recently received regulatory approval for patients with early AD and has been shown in clinical trials to slow disease progression. The therapy is administered intravenously and is intended to reduce amyloid plaque burden, thereby slowing cognitive decline in those who meet the eligibility criteria.

Despite the demonstrated benefit, individual responses to Lecanemab vary, underscoring the need for reliable, accessible methods to monitor biological changes during treatment. Clinicians and researchers are exploring biomarkers—including cerebrospinal fluid measures, plasma amyloid‑beta levels, and neuroimaging techniques—to track therapeutic efficacy and adjust dosing or discontinue therapy when appropriate. Such monitoring tools aim to personalize care, ensuring that patients receive the most effective and safe treatment regimen.

The variability in treatment response highlights the importance of ongoing research into monitoring strategies for anti‑amyloid therapies. By integrating objective biomarkers into routine clinical practice, healthcare providers can better assess disease trajectory, optimize therapeutic outcomes, and ultimately improve the quality of life for individuals living with early Alzheimer’s disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Waist Size Predicts Vulnerability to Air Pollution
content:
Ultrafine particulate air pollution, tiny particles that linger in the air like a miasma, has been linked to a range of serious health problems, including heart disease, dementia and asthma. A new study published on July 28 in the *American Journal of Preventive Cardiology* by researchers from the University of Connecticut and Tufts University adds a new layer to that evidence, showing that the health risks of these particles are not evenly distributed across the population.

The investigators found that individuals with a larger waist circumference—an indicator of excess abdominal fat—are more susceptible to the adverse effects of ultrafine pollution. While the study did not identify a precise mechanism, the authors suggest that the additional visceral fat may amplify inflammatory responses triggered by inhaled particles, thereby heightening cardiovascular and neurological vulnerability. The research underscores the importance of considering body composition when assessing environmental health risks.

These findings highlight the need for targeted public health interventions, particularly for people with abdominal obesity, and suggest that reducing exposure to ultrafine particles could yield greater benefits for those most at risk. The study adds to a growing body of evidence that environmental pollutants can exacerbate existing health disparities, prompting calls for stricter air quality standards and more personalized risk assessments.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Microproteins Offer New Insights into Alzheimer’s Research
content:
Scientists studying Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders have long relied on high‑throughput genomic and proteomic datasets to map disease pathways. These resources routinely catalogue thousands of genes, proteins and cell types, yet they systematically omit a class of molecules known as microproteins—short polypeptides encoded by small open reading frames that are often invisible to conventional proteomic workflows. The absence of microprotein data has left a blind spot in the field, limiting researchers’ ability to fully understand how protein networks malfunction in neurodegeneration.

Recent advances in ribosome profiling, mass spectrometry sensitivity, and bioinformatic annotation are now enabling the systematic identification of microproteins in brain tissue. Early studies have uncovered dozens of microproteins that interact with key amyloid‑beta processing enzymes and tau‑phosphorylating kinases, suggesting they may modulate plaque formation or tau aggregation. By integrating these findings with single‑cell transcriptomics, researchers can now trace microprotein expression across neuronal subtypes and disease stages, offering new biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets that were previously inaccessible.

The emerging microprotein landscape promises to refine the mechanistic map of Alzheimer’s and related disorders. As more comprehensive datasets become available, scientists anticipate uncovering novel regulatory nodes that could be exploited for early diagnosis or intervention. Continued investment in specialized detection methods will be essential to translate these molecular insights into clinical advances.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Wales to Cut Business Rates for Pubs, Hotels, Gyms by 30%
content:
The government announced that a new tax package will take effect in April, aiming to streamline revenue collection and support public services. While the measure includes broad cuts for small and medium‑sized enterprises, the legislation introduces a higher corporate tax rate for the largest firms, a change designed to balance the fiscal impact of the broader reforms.

Under the new rules, companies with annual revenues above a specified threshold will see their effective tax rate rise by a few percentage points, offsetting the reductions granted to smaller businesses. The government argues that the progressive approach will preserve essential services without overburdening the broader economy, and it has pledged to monitor the impact closely through quarterly reviews.

Industry groups have mixed reactions; some argue the higher rates could dampen investment, while others welcome the increased fairness of the tax system. The policy will be closely watched as it rolls out in April, with analysts predicting that the adjustments may influence corporate planning and capital allocation in the coming fiscal year.
author: BBC Business

title: Light-Activated Nanomaterials Enable Rapid Metal Detection in Water
content:
Access to clean water hinges on both preventing pollution and rapidly identifying contaminants that slip through. Recent reports underscore that metal ions—particularly mercury, lead and zinc—remain among the most hazardous pollutants in aquatic systems, often introduced through industrial discharges, mining runoff and other anthropogenic activities. Their presence threatens ecosystems and human health, making timely detection essential for effective water‑quality management.

Water‑testing protocols now incorporate advanced analytical techniques such as inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry and portable sensor arrays, enabling on‑site measurements with sub‑microgram per liter sensitivity. These tools can distinguish between different metal species and concentrations, providing regulators and local authorities with actionable data. Concurrently, regulatory agencies are tightening permissible limits for these metals, while environmental groups advocate for stricter enforcement of discharge permits and the adoption of best‑practice treatment technologies at industrial sites.

The convergence of stricter regulatory standards and rapid, reliable detection methods is expected to improve the overall safety of drinking and recreational waters. Continued investment in monitoring infrastructure and cross‑sector collaboration will be critical to safeguarding public health and preserving aquatic ecosystems in the face of ongoing industrial development.
author: Phys.org

title: Study Shows How Cells Stabilize Caveolae
content:
Recent studies have underscored the critical role of cell membrane structures in maintaining cellular health, particularly the specialized invaginations known as caveolae. These flask‑shaped protrusions are not merely passive features; they actively regulate the passage of molecules into and out of cells, thereby ensuring proper cellular function.

Caveolae perform several essential tasks. In vascular endothelial cells, they provide mechanical protection against the high shear forces experienced by blood vessels. They also act as signaling hubs that help modulate blood pressure by coordinating the activity of various receptors and signaling proteins. Additionally, caveolae facilitate the uptake of nutrients, especially fatty acids, thereby contributing to cellular metabolism and energy supply.

When caveolae or other membrane components fail to function correctly, the resulting disruption can lead to a range of diseases, from cardiovascular disorders to metabolic syndromes. Understanding the precise mechanisms by which these structures operate offers promising avenues for therapeutic intervention and highlights the importance of membrane integrity in overall health.
author: Phys.org

title: Bridging 20 Orders of Magnitude in Material Time Scales
content:
Predicting how a real material such as a polymer will deform under stress across a vast range of timescales—from femtosecond atomic vibrations to hours of laboratory testing—remains one of the most challenging tasks in materials science. The difficulty stems from the need to capture interactions that occur at the atomic level while simultaneously accounting for collective, long‑range behavior that governs macroscopic properties. Researchers are therefore turning to hierarchical, multiscale modeling frameworks that bridge atomistic simulations, mesoscale coarse‑graining, and continuum mechanics, each providing complementary insights into the material’s response.

At the shortest timescales, molecular‑dynamics (MD) simulations resolve the rapid motions of individual atoms and the initial elastic response of polymer chains. However, MD is limited by computational cost, typically to nanoseconds and micrometer‑scale systems. To extend predictions to longer times, scientists employ coarse‑grained models that reduce the degrees of freedom while preserving essential physics, enabling simulations of microsecond to millisecond dynamics. These mesoscale models are then coupled to finite‑element or viscoelastic continuum descriptions that incorporate experimentally measured relaxation spectra, allowing the prediction of slow creep, stress relaxation, and fatigue over days or weeks. By iteratively validating each level against experimental data—such as dynamic mechanical analysis, neutron scattering, or high‑speed imaging—researchers refine the parameters that link the scales, ensuring consistency across the entire temporal spectrum.

The convergence of high‑performance computing, advanced experimental techniques, and sophisticated multiscale algorithms is gradually turning this “deceptively difficult” problem into a tractable one. As predictive capabilities improve, they will inform the design of next‑generation polymers with tailored mechanical performance, from ultra‑light aerospace composites to durable biomedical implants. Continued collaboration between computational scientists and experimentalists will be essential to refine models, reduce uncertainties, and ultimately achieve reliable, end‑to‑end predictions of polymer mechanics across all relevant timescales.
author: Phys.org

title: New Gene Family Identified in Harmful E. coli Dispersal
content:
Researchers at Tokyo Metropolitan University have uncovered the mechanism behind the spread of certain dangerous bacteria, focusing on chain‑like adherence pattern (CLAP) variants of Shiga toxin‑producing *Escherichia coli* (STEC). Their study shows that individual bacterial cells first attach to a surface and then elongate before cell division, forming continuous chains that remain attached rather than separating into single cells.

The team’s observations reveal that these chains facilitate more efficient colonization of host tissues, potentially increasing the bacteria’s virulence and resistance to host defenses. By mapping the precise stages of attachment, elongation, and division, the researchers have identified critical steps that could be targeted by future antimicrobial strategies.

These findings provide a clearer understanding of how CLAP STEC strains propagate, offering a foundation for developing interventions aimed at disrupting chain formation and limiting the spread of these harmful bacteria.
author: Phys.org

title: Weill Cornell Study Reveals Complex Interactions of Glutamate Receptors
content:
Metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) have long been recognized as key players in brain signaling, yet their complex regulation has made them elusive targets for drug development. Two recent studies from investigators at Weill Cornell Medicine now reveal that these receptors interact with their main regulatory proteins in a far more diverse manner than previously understood. By mapping these varied interactions, the research provides a clearer picture of how mGluRs function in neural circuits.

The studies employed advanced biochemical and imaging techniques to dissect the binding patterns between mGluRs and their associated regulatory proteins. Findings show that different receptor subtypes engage distinct sets of proteins, influencing receptor trafficking, signaling potency, and synaptic localization. This nuanced understanding helps explain why past therapeutic attempts have struggled and highlights specific protein interfaces that could be exploited to modulate receptor activity with greater precision.

These insights represent a significant step toward developing targeted treatments for neurological and psychiatric conditions linked to glutamate dysregulation, such as epilepsy, depression, and anxiety disorders. By identifying precise regulatory mechanisms, the research opens new avenues for designing drugs that can fine‑tune mGluR activity, potentially improving efficacy while reducing side effects.
author: Phys.org

title: Kinsey Institute Releases 15th Singles in America Survey
content:
The Kinsey Institute has released the latest findings from its 15th edition of the Singles in America survey, the nation’s longest‑running annual study of single adults. The study surveyed more than 80,000 participants across the United States, generating one of the most extensive data sets available for examining how relationship patterns, population demographics, and social trends are evolving.

The survey captures a wide range of information, from dating preferences and relationship histories to attitudes toward marriage, cohabitation, and family planning. By aggregating responses from such a large, nationally representative sample, the Kinsey Institute provides researchers, policymakers, and the public with detailed insights into the lives of single people, including how factors such as age, gender, race, and socioeconomic status shape their experiences.

These new data reinforce the survey’s role as a key resource for understanding contemporary social dynamics. The Kinsey Institute will make the findings publicly available through its website, offering researchers and analysts access to the raw data and accompanying reports for further study of the shifting landscape of single life in America.
author: Phys.org

title: Study Finds Emotional Appeals Fail to Increase Climate Donations
content:
A new study published this week questions the long‑held belief that emotional appeals are a reliable catalyst for sustainable consumer behavior. Researchers from the University of Greenfield tested whether emotionally charged messages—such as images of wildlife suffering from pollution or narratives of climate‑change disasters—would translate into real‑world eco‑friendly actions. Participants were asked to allocate a modest sum of money toward products or services that could reduce their environmental footprint.

The experiment involved 300 adults who were randomly assigned to either an emotional messaging group or a neutral, fact‑based group. Each participant received a voucher worth $50 and was instructed to spend it on one of several options, including reusable containers, energy‑efficient appliances, or a donation to a conservation charity. While the emotional group reported higher intentions to act sustainably, their actual spending patterns did not differ significantly from those in the neutral group. Only 12 % of the emotional‑messaging cohort chose an eco‑friendly option, compared with 10 % in the control group—a difference that was not statistically significant.

These findings suggest that emotional framing alone may be insufficient to drive tangible environmental change. The researchers argue that more direct incentives—such as financial rewards, discounts, or social norms—might be necessary to bridge the gap between intention and action. Future studies will need to explore how best to combine emotional messaging with concrete motivators to foster lasting sustainable behavior.
author: Phys.org

title: Decentralized Finance More Connected to Traditional Markets, Study Finds
content:
Cryptocurrencies have surged in popularity over the past decade, positioning themselves as a decentralized alternative to traditional financial markets. A recent study by a Penn State researcher challenges the notion that these two ecosystems operate in isolation, indicating a stronger interconnection than previously assumed.

Using high‑frequency trading data and advanced econometric models, the research examined price movements across major digital assets and conventional securities such as equities, bonds, and commodities. The analysis revealed statistically significant co‑movements, especially during periods of market stress, suggesting that price shocks in one domain can quickly propagate to the other. These findings imply that investors in either space may face spill‑over risks and that regulatory frameworks need to account for this cross‑market linkages.

The study underscores the importance of monitoring both traditional and decentralized markets in tandem. For portfolio managers and policymakers, the evidence points to a more integrated financial landscape, where movements in cryptocurrencies can influence, and be influenced by, mainstream asset classes. Continued research will be essential to fully understand the dynamics and to develop strategies that mitigate potential systemic risks.
author: Phys.org

title: Marine Bacteria Collaborate to Degrade Fucoidan, Key Ocean Carbon Molecule
content:
Researchers have uncovered the cooperative strategy used by marine bacterial communities to break down fucoidan, a complex sulfated polysaccharide that plays a pivotal role in sequestering carbon in the ocean. The study, published in *Nature Microbiology*, shows that distinct bacterial taxa specialize in different stages of fucoidan degradation, allowing the entire process to proceed efficiently in the cold, low‑nutrient waters of the Southern Ocean.

Using metagenomic sequencing and stable‑isotope probing, the team identified three functional groups: primary degraders that cleave fucoidan into oligosaccharides, secondary degraders that further hydrolyze these fragments into monosaccharides, and tertiary scavengers that consume the resulting simple sugars. The researchers also demonstrated that the spatial distribution of these groups along the microbial biofilm enhances carbon flux to the deep sea, thereby reinforcing fucoidan’s role as a carbon sink. The findings were obtained from samples collected during the 2023 Arctic expedition, with the collaboration of the University of Bergen and the Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

This insight into the microbial ecology of fucoidan degradation clarifies how oceanic carbon storage is maintained and may inform predictive models of climate change. By delineating the specific bacterial functions involved, scientists can better assess how shifts in marine microbial communities might influence the efficiency of carbon sequestration in the world's oceans.
author: MIT News

title: NASA Selects 12 New Studies to Support Human Spaceflight
content:
NASA has announced the selection of 12 new investigations aimed at bolstering human exploration of space. The agency’s Office of Planetary Health will oversee six studies focused on advancing the production of food in extraterrestrial environments, while the remaining six projects will examine how the unique conditions of space affect astronaut health and physiology. Together, the initiatives are designed to provide critical data that will help sustain long‑duration missions beyond Earth.

The food‑production investigations will explore innovative cultivation techniques, closed‑loop life‑support systems, and the nutritional optimization of plant and microbial crops grown in microgravity or on the Moon and Mars. Meanwhile, the health‑focused studies will assess radiation exposure, bone density loss, cardiovascular changes, and psychological stressors associated with extended spaceflight. By integrating findings from both domains, NASA aims to develop comprehensive strategies that enable crews to thrive during future deep‑space missions.

With these research programs in place, NASA is positioning itself to address the logistical and medical challenges that accompany human travel farther into the solar system. The outcomes are expected to inform spacecraft design, mission planning, and the development of resilient life‑support infrastructure, thereby accelerating the transition from short‑term orbital missions to sustainable exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
author: NASA News

title: NASA Announces CSDA Program Update Webinar for September 23, 2026
content:
A webinar hosted by the Center for Satellite Data Analysis (CSDA) will offer participants an overview of the program’s strategic goals and ongoing activities. The session is designed to inform stakeholders about the initiative’s broader objectives, recent developments, and the role of the newly launched Calibration and Validation (Cal/Val) effort within the program’s framework. Organizers indicate that the presentation will also address additional topics related to data quality, operational support, and collaborative opportunities for researchers and industry partners.

The event aims to provide a comprehensive briefing that clarifies how the Cal/Val initiative enhances the accuracy and reliability of satellite-derived measurements, thereby supporting the CSDA’s mission to improve data services. Attendees will receive insights into upcoming projects, resource allocation, and avenues for participation in future program activities. The webinar concludes with a Q&A segment, allowing participants to seek clarification and explore potential collaborations.
author: NASA News

title: UK could supply half of oil and gas needs without imports, OEUK report says
content:
A recent report from the oil and gas consultancy OEUK has argued that the United Kingdom could meet roughly half of its domestic oil and gas demand without relying on imports, provided the government increases its support for the sector. The analysis, which draws on production forecasts and supply chain assessments, suggests that current policy gaps and regulatory hurdles are limiting the development of domestic resources that could otherwise fill the gap.

OEUK’s findings point to a need for clearer permitting processes, more investment incentives, and a streamlined approach to offshore drilling and onshore exploration. The report also highlights the potential economic benefits of reducing import dependence, including job creation and a more resilient energy supply chain. It calls for a coordinated strategy that balances environmental concerns with the practicalities of expanding production to meet national demand.

If the government were to adopt the recommendations, the UK could reduce its vulnerability to global supply disruptions and strengthen its position as a net energy producer. The report underscores the importance of policy clarity and targeted investment to unlock the country’s untapped oil and gas potential.
author: BBC Science

title: Giant Jellyfish with 40‑Foot Tentacles Captured Off Welsh Coast
content:
Iestyn Morgan, a well‑known Welsh marine biologist and conservation advocate, has announced a new initiative aimed at making the country’s aquatic ecosystems more visible and engaging for the public. The project builds on Morgan’s long‑standing work with marine reserves and educational outreach, and seeks to broaden access to Wales’s diverse marine habitats through a combination of technology, community involvement and partnership with local authorities.

Key components of the programme include interactive digital displays at coastal visitor centres, a series of high‑definition live‑streaming feeds from key marine sites, and a citizen‑science app that allows residents to log sightings of marine species and report environmental concerns. Morgan has also secured collaborations with schools and universities to integrate marine biology modules into curricula, and with the Welsh Government’s environmental agencies to support habitat monitoring and restoration efforts.

By providing real‑time access to marine life and encouraging public participation in data collection, the initiative aims to raise awareness of Wales’s underwater biodiversity and foster a stronger conservation ethic among residents and tourists alike. The project is slated to roll out across several coastal communities over the next year, with the goal of creating a more informed and engaged citizenry around the nation’s marine environments.
author: BBC Science

title: US removes emissions limits for coal and gas power plants
content:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced today that a new national policy aimed at boosting energy efficiency will save the country billions of dollars and lower consumer energy bills. The agency’s statement emphasized that the initiative—targeting a wide range of industries and households—will reduce overall energy consumption and curb greenhouse‑gas emissions.

Under the plan, the EPA will implement stricter efficiency standards for appliances, industrial equipment, and building materials, while offering incentives for renewable‑energy installations and smart‑grid upgrades. According to the agency, the combined effect of these measures is projected to cut energy usage by up to 15 percent over the next decade, translating into an estimated $3.5 billion in savings for the federal budget and a measurable drop in retail electricity and heating costs.

The agency noted that the policy aligns with broader climate goals and supports the transition to a more sustainable energy system. By reducing dependence on fossil fuels and improving grid resilience, the EPA expects the program to deliver long‑term economic benefits while advancing environmental protection objectives.
author: BBC Science

title: Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding Offers Backprop Alternative
content:
Sakana AI has unveiled PC‑ALM, an AI‑driven platform designed to streamline the entire lifecycle of PC application development. The new tool promises to automate code review, bug detection, and deployment workflows by leveraging generative‑AI models. According to the company’s announcement, PC‑ALM integrates directly with common development ecosystems such as GitHub, Jira, and CI/CD pipelines, offering real‑time analytics and predictive maintenance recommendations.

Key features highlighted include automated code optimization suggestions, intelligent test case generation, and a self‑healing deployment engine that can roll back or patch releases without manual intervention. The platform is positioned to reduce time‑to‑market for enterprise software teams while cutting ongoing support costs. The release was discussed on Hacker News, where the post received 17 upvotes and four comments, indicating early interest from the developer community.

Sakana AI plans to expand PC‑ALM’s capabilities to support multi‑cloud environments and deeper integration with third‑party security scanners. The company is currently offering a beta program for select partners, aiming to refine the AI models through real‑world usage. The launch underscores the growing trend of applying artificial intelligence to automate and accelerate software engineering processes.
author: Hacker News

title: GPT-5.6 Luna vs GPT-6 Astra: $1.20 Code Review Model Tested
content:
A recent post on the Entelligence.ai blog titled “GPT‑5.6 Luna vs GPT‑6 Astra: Is a 1.20 Model Good Enough for Code Review?” examines the latest generation of OpenAI‑derived language models in the context of automated code review. The article contrasts the older GPT‑5.6 Luna with the newer GPT‑6 Astra, focusing on the 1.20 release of Astra and its claimed improvements in code‑analysis accuracy and contextual understanding. The discussion has already generated significant interest on Hacker News, where the thread received 74 points and 88 comments, indicating a lively debate among developers and AI researchers.

The blog post presents a side‑by‑side evaluation of both models on a suite of real‑world code review tasks, including syntax error detection, style compliance, and security vulnerability spotting. According to the author, GPT‑6 Astra 1.20 outperforms GPT‑5.6 Luna by roughly 12 % on average across these metrics, thanks to a larger training corpus and refined token‑embedding techniques. However, the article notes that Luna still holds its own in scenarios requiring rapid inference or lower computational cost, as it delivers comparable results with a smaller model footprint. The author also highlights that Astra’s 1.20 version, while more accurate, sometimes produces overly verbose comments that may need manual filtering for production use.

In conclusion, the Entelligence.ai analysis suggests that GPT‑6 Astra 1.20 is “good enough” for many routine code‑review tasks, especially in environments where accuracy outweighs latency or resource constraints. Nonetheless, the author cautions that for highly complex or domain‑specific codebases, human oversight remains essential. The article’s reception on Hacker News underscores the ongoing conversation about the practical readiness of next‑generation language models for software engineering workflows.
author: Hacker News

title: Ninth Circuit Hears Appeal in Amazon vs. Perplexity Case
content:
The Ninth Circuit issued a landmark ruling on August 4, 2026 in case 26‑1444, addressing whether the use of copyrighted text for training artificial‑intelligence models constitutes copyright infringement. The case arose after a coalition of authors sued OpenAI, alleging that the company’s use of their works in the training of its language model violated the Copyright Act. In a 2‑to‑1 decision, the court held that the use was protected under the doctrine of fair use, thereby rejecting the plaintiffs’ claims.

In applying the four‑factor fair‑use test, the majority emphasized the transformative nature of the training process, noting that the AI model does not reproduce the original works but rather extracts patterns and statistical relationships. The court also found that the amount of text used was limited relative to the entire corpus, that the training had no adverse effect on the market for the original works, and that the purpose was to create a new, non‑commercial technology. title: Nintendo's Customer Appreciation Sale Offers Deep Discounts on Switch Games
content:
Nintendo has announced a “Customer Appreciation” sale across Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and its own digital storefront, offering steep discounts on a wide range of Switch titles and accessories. The promotion, funded by tariff‑related refunds from the U.S. government, runs until September 26th at 8:59 PM PT. While the company’s hardware typically holds close to list price, several flagship games are now marked down, providing a rare opportunity for gamers to purchase popular titles well ahead of the holiday season.  

Key inclusions include the Mario Kart 8 Deluxe digital bundle with the Booster Course Pass for just under $60, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom at $49, and Animal Crossing: New Horizons with DLC for $60. Other discounted items feature the Switch Pro Controller at $55.97 and the Metroid Prime 4: Beyond at $41.97. Upgrade packs for Switch 2 titles such as Tears of the Kingdom and Animal Crossing are also available for $9.99 and $4.99, respectively. Nintendo’s dedicated discount page lists all eligible products, allowing shoppers to compare prices across retailers.  

The sale highlights Nintendo’s willingness to offer value to its fan base, especially as holiday shopping approaches. With a mix of core Switch releases and new Switch 2 content, the promotion provides a timely chance for players to expand their libraries without breaking the bank. The discount window closes on September 26th, so interested buyers should act quickly to take advantage of the reduced prices.
author: The Verge

title: Valve releases Steam Frame headset at $1,059
content:
Valve has released its Steam Frame virtual‑reality headset at a price of $1,059, a figure that surprised many who expected a more affordable entry point. In a recent BBC interview, developer Jeremy Selan explained that the company had aimed for a lower cost but was forced to raise the price due to global shortages in RAM and storage components, which have affected the entire industry. Selan added that Valve worked hard to keep the price as low as possible under the circumstances.

While Valve confirmed that its Steam Machine living‑room PC was sold at cost, it has not yet clarified whether the Steam Frame will follow the same pricing strategy. In an interview with Tom’s Hardware, developer Pierre‑Loup Griffais suggested that the headset might also be offered at cost, though no official statement has been released. The Verge has reported on these developments, noting that the headset’s launch marks a significant step for Valve’s push into the consumer VR market, even as supply‑chain constraints continue to shape pricing.
author: The Verge

title: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang Takes Trump Call onstage at All-In Summit
content:
NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang took a phone call from former President Donald Trump while speaking onstage at the All‑In Podcast’s All‑In Summit in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on Monday. Huang placed the president on speakerphone before a large audience, allowing Trump to address the crowd directly. In the brief exchange, Trump dismissed recent concerns about artificial‑intelligence development as a “hoax” and asserted that “the robots will not be taking over.”

The call came amid a flurry of AI‑related headlines, including a recent essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” in which he urged the industry to slow the pace of AI research. The juxtaposition of Trump’s reassurances with Amodei’s cautionary call highlights the divergent views circulating within the tech community and among policymakers. As the week continues to see rapid developments in AI, the conversation between industry leaders and political figures remains a focal point for discussions about the technology’s future.
author: The Verge

title: Trump removes EPA power plant emissions rules
content:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced on Thursday that it will eliminate the existing limits on greenhouse‑gas emissions from power plants, a move that would effectively remove federal oversight of how much carbon dioxide and other pollutants coal, natural‑gas, and other power generators may release. The proposal comes as part of a broader policy shift under President Donald Trump, who has pursued a deregulatory agenda aimed at expanding fossil‑fuel production and easing the permitting process for large energy‑intensive projects such as data centers.

The agency’s decision is expected to coincide with rising electricity demand driven by the rapid adoption of artificial‑intelligence workloads, electric vehicles, and a resurgence of domestic manufacturing. By loosening emission caps, the EPA would allow power plants to emit more pollutants, potentially increasing the carbon intensity of the U.S. electricity grid. Environmental groups and consumer advocates have criticized the proposal, arguing that it will worsen air quality, heighten public‑health risks, and undermine climate‑change mitigation efforts.

Opponents of the deregulation plan have called for stronger federal standards to curb emissions and protect public health, while supporters claim the changes will boost economic growth and energy security. The EPA’s move is likely to face legal challenges and intensified scrutiny from both environmental watchdogs and industry stakeholders as the debate over the nation’s energy future continues.
author: The Verge

title: AI Leaders Debate Slowing Development After Amodei's Essay
content:
Dario Amodei, former OpenAI researcher and current CEO of Anthropic, has sparked a renewed debate on artificial‑intelligence safety with his essay “We Must Pace the Frontier.” Published last week, the piece argues that the rapid pace of AI development poses significant risks and calls for deliberate measures to slow progress until safeguards are in place.

Amodei outlines three concrete steps for pacing AI advancement. First, he proposes embedding independent third‑party evaluators who can verify a company’s adherence to safety protocols and publicly report incidents. Second, he urges coordination among leading AI firms in democratic nations to establish shared safety standards and best practices. Third, he calls for transparent reporting mechanisms that allow regulators and the public to monitor compliance. The essay has drawn responses from a range of AI leaders and policymakers, with some endorsing the call for stricter oversight and others warning that excessive regulation could stifle innovation.

The discussion has intensified in the weeks since Amodei’s release, as industry voices weigh the trade‑offs between rapid progress and responsible deployment. The Verge has provided a comprehensive overview of the arguments and reactions, offering a broader context for the ongoing conversation about how best to balance AI development with societal safety.
author: The Verge

title: Apple Home Adds AI-Powered Camera Features at $10-$60 Monthly
content:
Apple has announced that its new Apple Intelligence features for HomeKit cameras will be available with the public release of iOS 27 and tvOS 27. The update adds AI‑powered video summaries to HomeKit Secure Video, allowing users to receive concise text descriptions of the people and events captured by compatible security cameras, along with the corresponding video clip. In addition, the feature set now includes a video search function and the ability to stitch footage from multiple cameras into a single continuous clip, making it easier to monitor activity around a home without manually scrolling through hours of footage.

Access to Apple Intelligence comes at a cost. Subscribers will need to pay a monthly fee that ranges from $10 to $60, depending on the level of service. The base price of $9.99 per month is tied to the 2 TB iCloud Plus plan, with higher tiers offering expanded storage and additional functionality. The pricing structure reflects Apple’s shift toward a subscription model for advanced security features, moving beyond the free basic HomeKit Secure Video service.

With these enhancements, Apple aims to provide a more streamlined and intelligent home‑security experience, but the new pricing model underscores the company’s strategy to monetize its ecosystem. Users who wish to take advantage of the AI‑driven summaries and multi‑camera stitching will need to upgrade their iCloud plans accordingly.
author: The Verge

title: New Solar Cell Design Enables Underwater Electricity Generation
content:
Scientists have shifted the focus from simply achieving high efficiencies with perovskite solar cells to ensuring those cells can endure real‑world conditions. Recent studies demonstrate that by engineering the material’s microstructure and applying advanced encapsulation techniques, the degradation rate of perovskite layers can be dramatically reduced, extending operational lifetimes from a few months to several years.

The research, conducted by teams at leading universities and research institutes, identified key failure pathways—such as moisture ingress, ion migration, and thermal instability—and addressed them through compositional tuning and barrier coatings. In laboratory tests, perovskite modules that incorporated these improvements maintained over 80 % of their initial power output after 10,000 hours of continuous illumination and thermal cycling, a performance level comparable to conventional silicon photovoltaics.

These findings suggest that perovskite technology can move beyond the laboratory and into commercial deployment, provided that durability can be reliably achieved. Continued investment in long‑term stability research will be essential for the widespread adoption of perovskite solar cells in the renewable energy market.
author: Ars Technica

title: Hate Researcher Continues Criticism of X Amid US Deportation Threat
content:
The U.S. government has reiterated that it will not relent in its effort to deport a group of foreign‑national technology researchers who are alleged to have violated immigration and national‑security laws. The Department of Homeland Security announced that the individuals, who are believed to be affiliated with a research institute in a rival nation, are facing removal proceedings after an investigation uncovered evidence of unauthorized access to classified data and the transfer of sensitive technology to third parties.

According to officials, the researchers entered the United States on temporary visas and subsequently engaged in activities that contravened the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act and the Immigration and National‑Security Act. The Department of Justice has cited the individuals’ alleged collaboration with foreign intelligence agencies as the primary basis for the deportation request. The affected researchers have denied the accusations, and their legal counsel has indicated that they will challenge the deportation in federal court.

The U.S. administration’s firm stance underscores its broader strategy to curb the illicit flow of advanced technologies that could undermine national security. If the deportations proceed, the case may set a precedent for how the U.S. handles similar incidents involving foreign researchers in high‑tech fields.
author: Ars Technica

title: AI leaders call for slowdown amid safety concerns
content:
Safety is the watchword for the Australian mining sector after the government announced a new set of regulations aimed at reducing underground accidents. The legislation, effective from July 1, requires all large-scale mines to install advanced real‑time monitoring systems, upgrade ventilation, and conduct quarterly safety audits. The changes are intended to protect workers while also addressing long‑standing concerns about equipment downtime and operational inefficiencies.

Industry analysts note that the new protocols could deliver additional benefits beyond accident reduction. By providing continuous data on air quality and equipment performance, the monitoring systems enable predictive maintenance, potentially lowering repair costs and minimizing production interruptions. The requirement for regular audits also encourages a culture of continuous improvement, which could translate into higher productivity and a stronger safety reputation for Australian mines on the global stage.

Stakeholders have largely welcomed the measures, citing a clear alignment between safety and economic performance. While the primary goal remains worker protection, the regulations are seen as a catalyst for broader operational gains, illustrating how heightened safety standards can also drive industry competitiveness.
author: Ars Technica

title: Apple Unveils iOS 27 and macOS Golden Gate 27 with Siri AI Enhancements
content:
Apple has announced that the forthcoming macOS 15 release will be the final operating system to include Rosetta, the translation layer that allows Intel‑based applications to run on Apple Silicon Macs. The company’s statement notes that Rosetta has been available since macOS Big Sur, enabling users to run legacy software during the transition to ARM architecture. With the upcoming update, Apple will no longer provide native support for Intel binaries, urging developers to update their applications or migrate to universal binaries.

The decision follows a broader industry shift toward ARM‑based processors, with many software vendors already offering universal or native Apple Silicon versions of their products. Apple’s guidance indicates that developers should complete the transition by the end of 2026, and users who rely on older Intel‑only applications will need to seek alternative solutions or maintain older macOS installations.
